short: He refused terms in 1940 and made British defiance the turning point of the war.
full:
Winston Churchill became prime minister on 10 May 1940, the day the German offensive in the west began, and led a coalition drawn from all three parties. In the last week of that month he rejected Halifax's proposal to explore Italian-brokered terms, committing Britain to fight on after France fell. His speeches, and his careful cultivation of Roosevelt, held that position until the Soviet Union and the United States entered the war.

He directed strategy closely, sometimes disastrously, and attended the conferences at Tehran, Yalta and Potsdam that shaped the post-war settlement. The electorate removed him in July 1945 while Potsdam was still sitting. He returned in October 1951, aged seventy-six, presiding over the end of rationing and Britain's hydrogen bomb decision while concealing a serious stroke from the public, and resigned in April 1955. He had first entered Parliament in 1900.
